[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.303] Study 3

Study 3 aimed to replicate and extend Study 2. We followed people in daily life for twice as long as Study 2 to capture more instances of emotion regulation. Further, we assessed each strategy with two items to reduce error variance, addressing the limitation common to intensive longitudinal designs of assessing each construct with only one item.

In addition, encouraged by the results in Study 2 concerning the role that secret significance and negativity played in predicting regulatory processes, we investigated other features of secrets.
items.paper_content_summary: Study 3 aimed to replicate and extend Study 2, exploring strategy use and whether secret features predict regulation. It also reports between- and within-person variation and correlations. The discussion of features that might require greater regulation provides a rationale for exploration rather than a clearly stated directional hypothesis. [PREREG_0002, relevance_score=0.352] q2: We do not have formal hypotheses, but rather will investigate the following exploratory research questions:

4. Do certain features of the secret predict daily use of emotion regulation strategies to manage emotions about the secret?

[PAPER_0043, relevance_score=0.442] Design and Procedure

The study was approved by The University of Melbourne review board and had two consecutive parts. The baseline component worked in the same way as in Study 2. In the daily diary phase, participants completed a short survey about their experiences with their most important secret every evening for 14 consecutive days. Participants received a study notification via the Prolific platform every evening between 5:30 and 6:30 p.m. Daily surveys expired at midnight.

[PAPER_0063, relevance_score=0.311] Results

Descriptive Analyses

Descriptive statistics are shown in Tables 7 and 8 and Table S3.1 in the online supplemental materials . Echoing results from Study 2, the variance in emotion regulation strategies was relatively evenly split across between-person and within-person sources, with rumination showing the highest between-person variance (ICC = .56) and social sharing the least (ICC = .34). Table 9 shows between- and within-person correlations among variables of interest.
